article_title: Moving Beyond Reflection: Reflexivity and Epistemic Cognition in Teaching and Teacher Education
citation: Feucht, F. C., Lunn Brownlee, J., & Schraw, G. (2017). Moving beyond reflection: Reflexivity and epistemic cognition in teaching and teacher education. Educational Psychologist, 52(4), 234-241. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2017.1350180
title: The 3R-EC Framework: Reflection, Reflexivity and Resolved action for Epistemic Cognition
description: The 3R-EC Framework is a three-step process for changing teachers' epistemic cognition, adapted from Lunn and Schraw's original 3R Model and refined at a 2015 EARLI Advanced Study Colloquium. First, teachers 'identify a teaching issue of concern (Reflection)'; second, they engage in 'internal dialogue that included the weighing up of diverse structural, cultural and personal factors, including one's personal epistemologies (Reflexivity)'; third, 'decision making would be enacted in classroom contexts (Resolved action)'. The framework was retitled from 3R to 3R-EC to reflect the shift from personal epistemology to the broader construct of epistemic cognition, and served as the conceptual platform for the special issue's articles.
requirements: Teachers must identify a specific teaching issue of concern as the reflection step before internal dialogue and action can proceed
constraints: The framework is described as 'an evolving conceptual framework' whose theory-of-change for when, how and why epistemic cognition changes still requires empirical identification
target_learning_goals: changing epistemic cognition and personal epistemologies about knowledge and knowing
transformative change in classroom teaching practices
examples: The article by Lunn et al. in the special issue uses the framework to guide the process of developing a lesson plan in social studies
key_sources: Feucht, F. C., Lunn Brownlee, J., & Schraw, G. (2017). Moving beyond reflection: Reflexivity and epistemic cognition in teaching and teacher education. Educational Psychologist, 52(4), 234-241. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2017.1350180

article_title: Changing Teachers' Epistemic Cognition: A New Conceptual Framework for Epistemic Reflexivity
citation: Jo Lunn Brownlee, Leila E. Ferguson & Mary Ryan (2017). Changing Teachers' Epistemic Cognition: A New Conceptual Framework for Epistemic Reflexivity. Educational Psychologist, 52(4), 242–252. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2017.1333430
title: The 3R-EC Framework theorizes change in teachers' epistemic cognition through reflection, reflexivity, and resolved action
description: The 3R-EC Framework (Reflection, Reflexivity and Resolved Action for Epistemic Cognition) is a three-step model for changing teachers' epistemic cognition in specific teaching contexts. Step 1 involves reflecting on classroom practices and identifying associated epistemic aims; Step 2 involves reflexive deliberation calibrating practices with reliable processes for achieving those aims; Step 3 is resolved action. The article states that "The 3R-EC Framework for epistemic reflexivity focuses on making the epistemic aims and reliable processes explicit" and draws on Chinn and colleagues' AIR model to embed the epistemic in everyday teaching interactions.
requirements: Teachers identify epistemic aims embedded in teaching practices, not just the practices themselves
Examination of epistemic cognition in specific teaching and learning contexts rather than as broad epistemic beliefs
constraints: The authors do not suggest the framework would form the basis of every classroom interaction or lesson; it is described as useful for contested forms of knowledge and complex concepts
Its strength can be tested only through further empirical work such as longitudinal classroom interventions
target_learners: Student teachers in teacher education programs
target_learning_goals: Calibrating epistemic aims with teaching practices
examples: The framework is exemplified through teaching for active citizenship, where scenarios and provocations support children to reason about injustice, exclusion, and inclusion
key_sources: Jo Lunn Brownlee, Leila E. Ferguson & Mary Ryan (2017). Changing Teachers' Epistemic Cognition: A New Conceptual Framework for Epistemic Reflexivity. Educational Psychologist, 52(4), 242–252. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2017.1333430

article_title: Teachers' Epistemic Cognition in Classroom Assessment
citation: Fives, Helenrose, Barnes, Nicole, Buehl, Michelle, Mascadri, Julia, & Ziegler, Nathan. (2017). Teachers’ epistemic cognition in classroom assessment. Educational Psychologist, 52(4), pp. 270-283. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2017.1323218
title: 3R-EC model: a protocol for fostering reflexivity as an epistemic virtue targeting epistemic cognition
description: The 3R-EC model (Reflection-discernment, Reflexive-deliberation, Resolved Action-dedication, for Epistemic Cognition) is offered as a protocol for engaging teachers in reflexive practice aimed at epistemic cognition. The authors write that it "represents one protocol for fostering a disposition toward reflexive practice that targets epistemic cognition and can potentially be used to engage teachers in a habit of thinking about their assessment (and other teaching) practices with epistemic aims in mind." Reflexivity here extends reflection to a transformative level where understandings shift and actions are reconsidered.
requirements: A reflexive disposition, treated as an epistemic virtue, is positioned as necessary for teachers' epistemic cognition
constraints: The likelihood of routinely engaging in epistemic cognition may rest on the extent to which the individual has the epistemic virtue of a reflexive disposition
target_learning_goals: developing reflexive dispositions that support epistemic cognition in assessment practice
examples: The model is attributed to Brownlee Lunn, Ferguson, and Ryan and elaborated with the Dr. Jones assessment example
key_sources: Fives, Helenrose, Barnes, Nicole, Buehl, Michelle, Mascadri, Julia, & Ziegler, Nathan. (2017). Teachers’ epistemic cognition in classroom assessment. Educational Psychologist, 52(4), pp. 270-283. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2017.1323218
